**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Elias Voss* carved into the oak door of the old bookshop, I knew it wasn’t just a name. It was a promise—or a warning. The shop smelled of aged paper and something sharper, like ink left to dry in the corners of time. The owner, a gaunt man with fingers that moved like spider legs over the spines of books, told me the name meant *God is my help*, but his voice carried the weight of something unspoken. *Help from what?* I wondered.

I didn’t ask.

---

Books had always been my refuge. As a child, I devoured them like bread, swallowing whole the stories of kings and outcasts, of lovers who burned for each other across oceans and centuries. But words, I learned, could also be chains. The right ones could make a man forget his own name. The wrong ones could unravel him.

That’s what Elias Voss did.

I found him in the back room, surrounded by stacks of yellowed manuscripts, his face half-hidden behind a stack of ledgers. He didn’t look up when I entered. “You’re late,” he said, his voice like gravel underfoot. “The deal was for nine hundred words.”

I had brought a thousand.

“You’re not the first,” he murmured, flipping through a notebook. “But you’re the first who brought extra.”

I should have left then. Should have turned on my heel and walked out, the door creaking shut behind me like a ghost’s sigh. But I stayed.

Because Elias Voss wasn’t just a wordsmith. He was a thief.

---

The first time he took something from me, it was a memory.

I had been twelve, standing on the edge of a cliff by the sea, my father’s hand still warm in mine before he left for the war. The wind had carried the salt and the promise of something vast and untouchable. I had pressed my palm against the stone, feeling the cold seep into my bones, and whispered, *“I’ll remember this forever.”*

Elias Voss wrote it down.

Not in a notebook. Not in a place where I could find it. He wrote it into the margins of my own mind, where it festered like a bruise. The next time I closed my eyes, I saw the cliff—not as I had seen it, but as he had seen it. The sky wasn’t the endless blue I remembered. It was a bruise, too, split open with veins of gold.

*“You’ll forget,”* he had said, watching me. *“But I won’t.”*

---

He didn’t just take memories. He took *versions* of people. The way my mother laughed when she thought no one was listening. The way my brother’s hands trembled when he played the violin, the notes curling out of him like smoke. Elias Voss would sit in the corner of a room, unnoticed, and write them down. Then he would sell them.

Not to publishers. Not to historians. To *people*.

A woman who had never known laughter bought the version of my mother’s smile. A man who had lost his son to war paid for the way my brother’s fingers had danced over the strings. They took the words home like talismans, and for a little while, they believed.

I found out too late.

---

The last time I saw Elias Voss, he was standing in the middle of the bookshop, surrounded by a circle of strangers. They were all holding things he had given them—versions of lives they had never lived. Their faces were soft, their eyes bright with something like wonder.

“You’re not the first,” he said, turning to me. “But you’re the last.”

I should have run.

Instead, I asked, *“What do you want?”*

He smiled, slow and knowing. “The same thing I always do.”

He reached into his coat and pulled out a single sheet of paper. On it, in his precise, looping handwriting, was the story of my father’s last letter. The one I had never received. The one I had never known existed.

*“I’m sorry,”* it said. *“I’m coming home.”*

Elias Voss folded the paper and pressed it into my palm. “Take it,” he said. “Or leave it. But know this—words are the only things that never die.”

I burned the paper in the hearth that night.

The next morning, the bookshop was empty. The door stood ajar, as if waiting for someone who would never come back.

And I never saw Elias Voss again.

---

Sometimes, when the wind howls through the old streets, I swear I can still hear the scratch of his pen on paper. The sound of a name being carved into something deeper than wood.

*Elias Voss. God is my help.*

But the help never came.

And neither did I.
